pages.text: Innovation in the Agricultural and Food System | NBER Skip to main content Innovation in the Agricultural and Food System May 21, 2027 — Washington, DC Share X LinkedIn Facebook Bluesky Threads Email Link Over the past century, technological innovation has fundamentally reshaped US agriculture. Total output in this sector has increased manyfold even as labor use has declined dramatically. This remarkable productivity growth was sustained by mechanization, improvements in plant and animal genetics, expanded use of chemical fertilizers and pesticides, and advances in farm management practices. Modern production agriculture is increasingly connected to upstream input industries, downstream processing and retailing, data and financial services, and global supply chains. This agricultural and food system continues to create opportunities for innovation while also raising questions about incentives, market structure, technology adoption, risk, regulation, and the distribution of benefits. As society confronts the challenge of feeding a growing world population in an increasingly uncertain environment, it is essential to understand the economics of innovation throughout the agricultural and food system. What determines the direction and pace of innovation? How do new technologies diffuse across producers, firms, and regions? How do institutions and public policies shape innovation incentives? However, while air travel often feels simple and straightforward for passengers, every journey relies on a complex network of people, data, and technology working together to make it possible. As aviation evolves, this complexity does too. More passengers are taking to the skies, new technologies are entering the cockpit, and pilots have more data at their fingertips than ever before. The challenge is making sense of it all—harnessing the right information to make the right decisions at the right time. Not too long ago, pilots would begin their day by reading pages of flight information. Today, digital displays bring this information together, improving what pilots call situational awareness: their ability to build a clearer picture of what’s happening around them. All of which, “helps us make quicker, better decisions,” Jason Coffman, Commercial Airline Captain explains. Training has evolved too. Businesses can use input-output data to develop economic projections and forecasting models. Economists can use the data to examine the role of information technology on structural change, productivity, and the sources of economic growth. Researchers can use the data to analyze the economic effects of specific events. Input-output data are updated each year and provide information on 71 industry categories. Detailed benchmark input-output statistics, produced roughly every five years, are further subdivided into 402 industries. Benchmark input-output tables are fully integrated with the annual industry accounts and the national income and product accounts. Benchmark estimates at all levels of aggregation reflect the highly detailed and accurate data available during an economic census year. Release Information: Data released each September. The Houdini Chamber hosts 1920s-themed dinners. The Magic Castle By Zoey Goto Published October 31, 2026 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). From behind a plush velvet curtain, a magician steps into the spotlight. He’s dressed like a Victorian conjuror in a black frock coat, silk scarves billowing from his collar. To a flourish of orchestral music, a white dove suddenly appears in his outstretched hands, as if from thin air. Then another and another. Soon, five birds are fluttering around the stage in the jewel-box theatre. Before arriving at Hollywood’s Magic Castle, I thought I had a rudimentary understanding of magic. The smiling assistant sawn in half. The coin found behind an unsuspecting ear. The squidgy sponge ball tucked up a sleeve. But then I witnessed this master of illusion’s grand finale. Mondre the magician, a regular act at the Magic Castle, turns his empty palms towards the audience in a nothing-to-see-here gesture. Many of the spines sitting atop the animal’s tail vertebrae had been fractured. The dinosaur, known as Olorotitan to paleontologists, wasn’t simply clumsy; too many bones were broken. The breaks were more consistent with some heavy downward pressure right near the base of the tail. At 26 feet long and three tons, another Olorotitan would have been large enough to do such damage. Institute of Natural Sciences in Brussels paleontologist Filippo Bertozzo had ventured to Blagoveshchensk, Russia’s Paleontologic Museum in 2019 to study the dinosaur’s bones when he noticed the strange injuries. “When I realized what I had in front of me, I had a cry of joy,” says Bertozzo. He had seen busted bones like these before in his research and in the scientific literature—fractured vertebrate near the hadrosaur’s hips. In 1989, paleontologist Darren Tanke suggested that similar breaks were the result of mating as one dinosaur mounted the other. Few of them notice the keeper tossing the fish from a distance. Fewer still reflect on the equally important routine unfolding in the building across the pool. CPython implementation detail: DTrace markers are implementation details of the CPython interpreter. No guarantees are made about probe compatibility between versions of CPython. The account has proven useful for analysts studying structural change, globalization, the impact of information and communications technology, and the industry origins of productivity growth. pages.text: Interagency Wild & Scenic Rivers Council | Rivers.gov Skip to main content Interagency Wild & Scenic Rivers Council Image Details Stacy Shelton, FWS In 1993, at the celebration marking the 25th anniversary of the National Wild and Scenic Rivers System, conservation organizations challenged U.S. land management agencies to establish an interagency council to address the administration of our wild and scenic rivers. A few months later, in Portland, Oregon, river planners from the Bureau of Land Management, National Park Service, and U.S. Forest Service met to draft a rough outline of what such a council would look like and what it could do. In April of 1995, heads of these agencies and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, at a ceremony in Washington, D.C., signed the Interagency Wild & Scenic Rivers Coordinating Council Charter. Department of the Interior Assistant Secretaries George Frampton, Jr., and Robert Armstrong, and Department of Agriculture Undersecretary James Lyons then approved the Charter, thereby changing 25 years of managing wild and scenic rivers. The overriding goal of the Council is to improve interagency coordination in administering the Wild and Scenic Rivers Act, thereby improving service to the American public and enhancing protection of important river resources. The Council addresses a broad range of issues, from management concerns on rivers presently in the national system to potential additions listed on the Nationwide Rivers Inventory, from state designations to the provision of technical assistance to other governments and non-profits organizations

pages.description: InterCommunity is the Internet Society’s annual member meeting. Launched in 2015, our hybrid format brings our community together online and in-person for robust conversations about the issues and topics most relevant to us.
pages.text: InterCommunity - Internet Society InterCommunity InterCommunity is an event that gives the Internet Society community a way to connect and provide a space to discuss relevant issues. Since 2015, InterCommunity has brought us all together — online and in person — for meaningful conversations about the issues that matter most to the Internet. During InterCommunity 2018, we started to reshape the future of this event to make it more community focused so that we could increase our influence around the world. Feedback from the Community When we conducted a survey, you told us you wanted more ways to engage with other parts of the community, to share views and to exchange information. We also heard that you’re interested in finding more avenues for talking about Internet-related issues. Based on this feedback, InterCommunity evolved to become an online engagement platform, as well as a programme of events that run throughout the year. Rather than hosting a single global event in 2019, we hosted a series of quick-fire virtual roundtable webinars. This model is effective because it provides more scope for you to raise topics and issues that you’d like to cover. A New Format The new format provides more touchpoints, while being more inclusive. It creates opportunities for more consistent engagement and advocacy, and allows all of us to cover a for a broader range of meaningful topics. Intercountry (International) Adoption: Tuberculosis May 15, 2024 At a glance U.S. law requires parents who adopt children internationally to have their child screened for tuberculosis (TB). Learn more about TB and the types of tests your child will get during their overseas medical exam. About TB TB is caused by a bacterium called Mycobacterium tuberculosis that spreads through the air from one person to another when a person with TB disease of the lungs or throat coughs, speaks, or sings. The bacteria usually attack the lungs, but TB bacteria can attack any part of the body such as the kidneys, spine, and brain. Keep Reading Tuberculosis in Children TB disease is a serious condition. Worldwide, approximately 1.3 million people died of TB in 2022, including 167,000 people with HIV. In the United States, TB disease is less common than in many other countries.
